item.title: Response of GAGG(Ce) scintillators to different charged particles
item.description: arXiv:2610.14518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Charged-particle telescopes play an essential role in studies of nuclear clustering, which require high-resolution detection of charged breakup fragments. GAGG(Ce) is a promising scintillator for charged-particle detection at high counting rates because of its high light yield, fast response, and non-hygroscopic nature. However, systematic data on its light-output response to different charged particles remain scarce. In this work, we present a systematic study of the scintillation light-output response of GAGG(Ce) crystals to various charged particles and quantify the associated quenching behavior. The relationship between the scintillation light output and the deposited energy is established over a broad range of particle species and energies, providing essential experimental input for response modeling and energy calibration of GAGG(Ce)-based charged-particle detector systems.

item.title: Development of high-resolution timing technique in the past 25 years
item.description: arXiv:2610.14919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper reviews recent progress in high-resolution timing, rate capability, and aging performance of particle detectors in the context of developments over the past 25 years. It focuses on MCP, SiPM, LGAD, 3D silicon, and SiEM detectors and compares their performance with that of gaseous timing detectors. In addition, preliminary results from a simplified simulation program, Mini-TCAD, are presented, indicating that hexagonal 3D silicon cells may provide better drift-time uniformity and timing resolution than square cells.
item.dc:creator: Jerry Vavra

item.title: Broadband 600- and 1200-GHz Subharmonically Pumped Schottky Diode Mixers
item.description: arXiv:2610.15657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A subharmonic mixer topology is introduced that uses quarter-wave stubs to create virtual RF/LO grounds and provide impedance matching in close proximity to the antiparallel Schottky barrier diode pair, thereby reducing the electrical length and enabling broadband operation. The RF/LO matching topology is demonstrated at 600 GHz and 1200 GHz, with good agreement between measured and simulated performance. The 600-GHz mixer demonstrates approximately 20% RF bandwidth with a DSB receiver noise temperature below 1300 K across most of the measured band, while the 1200-GHz implementation achieves DSB receiver noise temperatures below 3000 K over a broad frequency range. Both mixers are characterized at room temperature with approximately 2 mW of LO power. The 600-GHz mixer is used in the Submillimeter Wave Instrument (SWI) onboard ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer. Overall, these results demonstrate state-of-the-art room-temperature performance for broadband receiver front ends targeting atmospheric research and remote-sensing applications.

item.title: A Low-Temperature Tool for Acousto-electric Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.16262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We have developed an apparatus for the measurement of the acousto-electric effect (AEE) from room temperature to liquid nitrogen temperatures. The AEE is excited by bulk acoustic waves (BAWs) for which a lithium niobate piezoelectric actuator is employed. A very low background noise level is realized through careful electrical and mechanical design of the setup. The validity of the setup is tested by measuring the AEE in heavily doped P-type and N-type silicon. The opposite sign of the AEE signal was seen for both samples, showing dependence of the signal on the type of charge carrier being dragged by acoustic waves. The signal showed quadratic dependence on the driving voltage, which is consistent with the AEE literature. Further, a temperature dependence of the AEE signal was measured, which exhibits a monotonic increase with a rise in temperature. The ability to probe the AEE in bulk samples at low temperatures makes this setup a promising tool to investigate the AEE and related phenomena in different materials at cryogenic temperatures.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Mandlik, Sunil Nair

item.title: Readout chain of SPD DAQ system
item.description: arXiv:2610.16515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Spin Physics Detector (SPD) experiment at the NICA collider of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) aims to study the spin structure of the nucleon and spin-related phenomena. The experimental conditions, including the high interaction rate and the large number of readout channels, require a triggerless data acquisition system with high throughput and a scalable architecture. This work presents a hardware implementation of the readout chain that extends the previously proposed SPD DAQ architecture. The chain is based on two levels of concentrators. The L1 concentrator provides the interface between the front-end electronics and the next system level and distributes synchronous signals. The L2 concentrator aggregates data streams from several L1 concentrators before transmitting them to the computing system. A key feature of the L2 implementation is the offloading of data reception, buffering, and aggregation from the host CPU to the FPGA, motivated by the large number of small packets generated by the readout electronics. The developed hardware platforms and their operating logic are presented, together with experimental results for the main interfaces and data-path components. The obtained results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed hardware architecture and its application in a scalable SPD data acquisition system.

item.title: FINESSE: A Versatile Beamline for Fundamental Interactions with Neutrons at the European Spallation SourcE
item.description: arXiv:2610.17373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: FINESSE (A Versatile Beamline for \textbf{F}undamental \textbf{I}nteractions with \textbf{N}eutrons at the \textbf{E}uropean \textbf{S}pallation \textbf{S}ourc\textbf{E}) is a proposed versatile beamline for fundamental interactions with neutrons at the European Spallation Source. Building on the HIBEAM design studies, FINESSE extends the original concept into a dual-guide beamline capable of operating either in a high-flux configuration or in a low-background configuration within a single ESS beam port. The high-flux branch is optimized for rare-process searches, including neutron--antineutron oscillations, neutron--sterile-neutron transitions, axion-like-particle searches, neutron charge measurements, and rare neutron decays. The low-background branch is designed for precision measurements requiring strong suppression of prompt and line-of-sight backgrounds, with a cryogenic neutron electric-dipole-moment experiment used as a benchmark case. A baseline exchangeable-guide concept has been developed in which only short guide sections inside the ESS bunker are exchanged, while the upstream extraction system and chopper positions remain fixed. A staged implementation, Short FINESSE, would use the upstream section of the high-flux beamline together with a compact magnetically controlled experimental region, enabling an early physics and R\&D programme before completion of the full facility. This paper summarizes the scientific case, beamline concept, guide simulations, chopper and timing system, magnetic-field control, detector developments, and staged implementation strategy. FINESSE would establish a long-term particle-physics infrastructure at ESS, providing a beamline for both discovery-driven searches and precision neutron measurements throughout the lifetime of the facility.

item.title: Performance and Radiation Damage of the Heavy-Ion Silicon Beam Tracker in the BM@N Experiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.17947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Silicon Beam Tracker (SiBT) of the BM@N experiment at the NICA complex (JINR, Dubna) is designed to reconstruct trajectories of beam ions upstream of the target. It consists of three stations based on double-sided silicon strip detectors (DSSDs) installed directly in the relativistic heavy-ion beam. The SiBT performance and radiation damage were studied using data from the 2026 experimental run with $^{124}$Xe beams at~$1.6$,~$2.2$, and~$3.0$~AGeV. During the run, the leakage current of the DSSD of the third station of SiBT increased by $28.95~\mu\mathrm{A}$, while the charge collection efficiency in the beam center decreased to approximately $68\%$ at the nominal bias voltage of 30~V. Increasing the bias voltage to 90~V restored the charge collection efficiency to approximately $95\%$. Despite the radiation-induced signal degradation, the tracking efficiency remained close to $99\%$. The accumulated radiation damage was also used to reconstruct the spatial distribution of the integrated beam fluence from strip-by-strip leakage-current measurements, yielding an average fluence of approximately $1.3\times10^{12}~\mathrm{n_{eq}/cm^2}$.

item.title: Cryogenic characterisation of the FBK NUV-HD-cryo Silicon Photomultipliers for the DarkSide-20k dark matter experiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.18223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) are highly promising detectors for dark matter searches due to their uniform response, scalability to large target masses, and compatibility with ultra-low background conditions. The DarkSide-20k (DS-20k) experiment, currently under construction at Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN) Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), aims to achieve unprecedented sensitivity to Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), approaching the neutrino fog. At the heart of the detector is a dual-phase TPC filled and surrounded by low-radioactivity argon from underground sources (i.e. Underground Argon (UAr)), functioning both as the WIMP target and detection medium. The experiment employs Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-cryo Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) as the chosen photon sensors for its optical planes. Key SiPM properties such as dark noise rate, gain and direct crosstalk were measured using specialized test setups at 77 K. The photon detection efficiency (PDE) was measured under vacuum at 77 K over the wavelength range 350-820 nm. Secondary photon emission, which can give rise to external optical crosstalk, was measured under vacuum at 86 K over the wavelength range 550-1020 nm.

item.title: The Energetic Particle Detector Instrument on ELFIN
item.description: arXiv:2610.18628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the design methodology, implementation, and data products of the Energetic Particle Detector (EPD) instrument on-board the Electron Losses and Fields Investigation (ELFIN) dual SmallSat mission. ELFIN was designed to study the time-evolution of energetic particle distributions in Earth's magnetosphere, having operated in polar Low Earth Orbit (LEO) from 2018 to 2022. Each satellite's instrument payload contained a pair of detector heads to sense differential-directional fluxes of 50 keV to $\sim$5 MeV electrons (EPDE), and 50 keV to $\sim$2 MeV atomic ions (EPDI), with an energy resolution better than 50% ($\Delta E/E<0.5$). The satellites were spinning with a nominal period of 2.8 s in a plane containing Earth's background magnetic field, with particle counting intervals subdivided into 16 consecutive spin sectors. Each EPD was paired with a three-axis Fluxgate Magnetometer (FGM) sampled at 80 Hz for local pitch-angle determination. Each detector head operated on the principle of pulse-height analysis (PHA) in solid state media, collimated by a rectangular 22.5$^\circ$ field of view and entrance aperture. The EPDE contained a stack of 6 silicon detectors (0.7 cm total thickness) with 0.15 cm$^2$ str geometric factor, with ion contamination mitigated by an aperture foil and digital coincidence logic. The EPDI contained a stack of 2 silicon detectors (0.1 cm total thickness) with 0.03 cm$^2$ str geometric factor, with electron contamination mitigated by a magnetic broom stage and digital anti-coincidence logic. The total assembled mass, volume, and power required for the EPD detector heads and circuit boards were 939 g, 10$\times$9.8$\times$8.4 cm$^3$, and 2.3 W, respectively. We describe each EPD design element alongside instrument data products and processing.

item.title: Energy, vertex, and time response of a LiquidO detector with an opaque-scintillator target to Compton-tagged electrons
item.description: arXiv:2610.18849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LiquidO detectors confine scintillation light near its point of production by stochastic scattering in an opaque medium and collect it with a lattice of wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers. The elementary signal of such a detector is the point-like sub-MeV energy deposition, yet the response to that signal at the center of the detector volume has not been measured against an event-by-event ground truth. To close this gap, we couple BPULSE, a 4-liter prototype LiquidO detector, to a Compton-coincidence calibration setup that selects electron recoils of known energy on a constrained beam axis. The prototype is a 160 mm cube of opaque scintillator with 64 WLS fibers in alternating orthogonal layers at a 20 mm pitch, read out by silicon photomultipliers. Compton scatters of collimated gamma-ray beams from $^{137}$Cs and $^{60}$Co sources are tagged by a NaI(Tl) spectrometer. For 373.4 keV electrons, tagged from $90^{\circ}$ scatters of the $^{137}$Cs beam, the detector collects $19.04 \pm 0.07$ photoelectrons (p.e.). Across four operating points, the two sources at two scattering angles, it responds linearly at $48.3 \pm 1.5$ p.e./MeV. The energy resolution of $(23.4 \pm 0.4)\%$ matches the Poisson statistics of the detected photoelectrons. Collection at both fiber ends and larger sensors would raise the light yield of this target to an estimated 108-124 p.e./MeV. Center-of-mass reconstruction locates each recoil to the width of the delivered 20 mm beam spot, which bounds the intrinsic localization of the detector from above. The arrival time response sets a lower bound of 1.5 ns on the single-scatter start time at the observed $\approx 19$ p.e. light level. This single-scatter response is the building block for reconstructing multi-site events. It constrains the light collection, confinement, and timing models on which reconstruction in future LiquidO detectors will rest.

item.title: Dual deconvolution multifocal fluorescence response matrix microscopy for aberration-free high-throughput super-resolution imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.15264v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fluorescence response matrix imaging enables separate computational correction of excitation and emission aberrations through dual deconvolution, but single-focus acquisition requires a large number of camera frames, limiting its practical use. Multifocal excitation can accelerate acquisition by recording many illumination positions in parallel, but denser foci also increase inter-focus crosstalk, which can bias the estimated excitation and emission optical transfer functions and degrade aberration correction. Here, we introduce high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging with adaptive multifocal illumination, in which the inter-focus spacing of the multifocal lattice is adjusted according to specimen-dependent crosstalk. A programmable digital micromirror device generates multifocal excitation lattices, and the resulting detector-resolved fluorescence responses are assembled into a two-coordinate fluorescence response matrix. Dual deconvolution separately estimates and corrects the excitation and emission optical transfer functions, and the aberration-corrected matrix is then combined in the spatial-frequency domain to reconstruct the aberration-free image. This strategy reduces the number of required camera frames by approximately three orders of magnitude, allowing response matrices with $\sim 10^6$ illumination positions to be acquired within seconds to a few minutes. The accelerated acquisition preserves the aberration-correction capability of dual deconvolution and achieves an estimated lateral resolution of $\sim$100 nm. Applied to heterogeneous mouse brain and kidney tissue, the method enables high-resolution, depth-resolved volumetric imaging while correcting specimen-dependent aberrations. Together, these results establish adaptive multifocal illumination as a practical route to high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging.

item.title: Universal Boolean Computation in Negatively Coupled Circle Map Lattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.16290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the computational capabilities of a one-dimensional lattice of negatively coupled circle maps in its traveling wave regime. We interpret propagating waves as information carriers and exploit their interactions to implement Boolean logic. The logical states are encoded by the propagation direction of the traveling waves, while the presence or absence of a wave at a designated output location represents the logical output. Using controlled wave collisions, we demonstrate the realization of NAND and NOR gates along with other basic gates. Since NAND and NOR operations are functionally complete, the results establish that the traveling wave regime of the negatively coupled circle-map lattice supports universal Boolean computation in principle. The demonstrated logical operations remain valid over a finite range of the coupling strength \epsilon and map parameter \omega, indicating robustness of the computational scheme to parameter variations. Our results therefore demonstrate that computational functionality can emerge from the collective nonlinear dynamics of a coupled map lattice, providing a con- nection between the dynamical properties of traveling wave states and collision based information processing.
item.dc:creator: Priyanka D. Bhoyar, Prashant M. Gade

item.title: Experimental Demonstration of Soft-Tissue Muon Scattering Tomography
item.description: arXiv:2610.16647v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Muons have fascinated physicists since their discovery in cosmic rays almost a century ago. Their large mass and relatively long lifetime allow relativistic muons to traverse large amounts of matter, a property that has been exploited to probe otherwise inaccessible structures, from volcanoes and archaeological monuments to shielded nuclear materials. Here, we experimentally demonstrate for the first time that muon scattering tomography can be extended to biological soft tissue. We image an anthropomorphic thorax phantom using a 2 GeV/c muon beam at the CERN Proton Synchrotron and reconstruct its three-dimensional scattering density from the measured deflections of individual muons. Despite the weak scattering produced by tissue-equivalent materials, the reconstructed density agrees with the expectation from simulation at the percent level. Our results extend muon imaging into a previously unexplored regime and open the possibility of using muons as a complementary probe for medical imaging.
item.dc:creator: Dipanwita Banerjee, Benjamin Banto Oberhauser, Paolo Crivelli, Laura Molina Bueno

item.title: 1/f frequency-noise reduction in nanomechanical resonators by dissipation dilution
item.description: arXiv:2610.16711v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The frequency noise of a resonant nanomechanical sensor is well understood down to its thermomechanical limit, but the longest useful averaging time is set by a flicker, or $1/f$, frequency-noise floor whose origin has remained unknown. We show that this floor is the thermal noise of the tension. By the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the tension of a resonator with fixed ends fluctuates by an amount set by the loss angle of its material; for structural damping, these fluctuations produce $1/f$ frequency noise with a flicker coefficient $h_{-1}=E k_{\mathrm{B}} T/(2\pi V\sigma_0^2 Q_{\mathrm{el}})$, with $Q_{\mathrm{el}}$ the intrinsic loss under elongation, that contains no free parameter and is diluted by the tensile stress $\sigma_0$ in the same way as damping is in dissipation dilution. Silicon nitride strings and membranes from 30 to 340~nm thickness follow the predicted volume scaling, the predicted $\sigma_0^{-2}$ dilution across resonators and within stress-engineered strings, and the predicted thickness dependence, which places noise-active two-level systems in the volume and at the surfaces of the resonators, all at the absolute level set by the independently measured intrinsic loss. The same relation accounts for published data between 78 and 296~K; below 78~K, the loss measured at the resonance no longer represents the loss probed by the noise, marking the limit of the structural-damping assumption. Dissipation dilution therefore lowers the $1/f$ floor, and the longest useful integration time of a resonant sensor is set by its prestress, volume, temperature, and intrinsic loss angle.

item.title: Anomaly Detection in Bunch Oscillations for Early Warning of Sudden Beam Loss at SuperKEKB
item.description: arXiv:2610.17241v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sudden beam loss (SBL) events at the SuperKEKB collider result in the loss of a large fraction of the stored beam within just a few revolutions, on a timescale comparable to or shorter than the 20-30 {\mu}s latency of the existing abort system. Such events have damaged collimators and threaten Belle II subdetectors. Bunch Oscillation Recorders (BORs) capture transverse bunch positions at each revolution, which often show sizable oscillations that precede significant beam current loss. We test whether these precursors can be detected earlier than a charge-based reference that mimics the existing abort sensors. We apply several oscillation-based anomaly detection algorithms to 208 SBL events recorded in the low-energy ring during the 2024 run period, ranging from simple rolling statistics to machine learning models trained to forecast bunch oscillation. On 173 events not used for training or calibration, the best-balanced model (DeepLSTM) triggers before the charge-based reference in 86-90% of events across five training seeds, with a mean lead time of 25-30 {\mu}s. The only trigger classified as a false alarm fires on an oscillation that begins about 60 turns before the abort and persists until the beam is lost, making it more likely an early precursor than a spurious trigger. These results establish bunch oscillations as a viable early abort trigger and motivate a shadow-mode deployment to measure the false-alarm rate in continuous operation.
item.dc:creator: H. Haigh, P. Horak, G. Inguglia, C. Krause, G. Mitsuka, H. Nakayama, R. Nomaru, M. Tobiyama

item.title: Non-contact lens metrology from optical flow and differentiable ray tracing
item.description: arXiv:2610.17515v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate lens surface metrology is essential to determine the manufactured geometry of refractive optical elements and their deviation from the specified design. We demonstrate a transmission metrology method that reconstructs refractive lens surfaces from the displacement of a wavelet-noise-patterned mask. Lens-induced distortion is represented by a dense displacement field. A differentiable ray tracer fits the lens geometry using a calibrated near-telecentric camera model with an effective finite ray origin. We validate the method on commercial lenses. The recovered geometries agree with nominal specifications, and the plano-aspheric reconstruction is compared with chromatic confocal profilometry.
item.dc:creator: Hector A. Jimenez-Romero, Wolfgang Heidrich

item.title: Mortality of ultra-thin LGADs and PiN diodes from high energy deposition
item.description: arXiv:2604.11571v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Low Gain Avalanche Diodes are prime candidates for high-resolution timing applications in High Energy Physics, Nuclear science, and several other fields. Operating these devices in high-radiation environments presents various hazards, including the risk of their permanent degradation or destruction caused by effects such as Single Event Burnout. Studies using minimum ionizing particles found a greatly reduced Single Event Burnout risk by operating below a bias voltage corresponding to an average electric field of 12 V/$\mu$m - however, as high energy particle colliders produce a wide energy spectrum of radiation, it is crucial to understand this phenomenon and other possible damage mechanisms at energy deposition levels greater than those of minimum ionizing particles. This was achieved by pre-irradiating LGADs and PiN diodes with active thicknesses of 20, 30, and 50 $\mu$m up to 1.5 $\times$ 10$^{15}$ $\mathrm{n_{eq}/cm^2}$, and exposing them to beams of protons and heavy ions (C, O, Fe, Au) at the BNL Tandem van de Graaff accelerator. Several mortality categories were observed, defined by different electrical and mechanical damage signatures. This furthers our understanding of permanent radiation damage of silicon devices, crucial towards mitigating Single Event Burnout and other damage mechanisms to safely operate future detectors.

item.title: Characterizing the energy resolution of the MicroBooNE LArTPC at the MeV scale using monoenergetic features of $^{208}$Tl decays
item.description: arXiv:2605.30709v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A detailed understanding of the capabilities and fidelity of low-energy reconstruction is crucial for taking advantage of MeV-scale neutrino physics opportunities in liquid argon time projection chambers (LArTPCs). This study presents a measurement of the resolution of reconstructed energy in the MicroBooNE LArTPC at $\approx 1.5$ MeV. The characterization is performed using monoenergetic signals generated by $2.614$ MeV $\gamma$-rays from $^{208}$Tl decays undergoing pair production in the detector. The resolution is found to be ($7.52 \pm 0.78 \text{(stat)} \pm 0.92 \text{(syst)}$)%. This value is consistent with the MicroBooNE simulation prediction of ($9.70 \pm 0.65 \text{(stat)}$)% at the $1.6 \sigma$ level. This study represents the first ever measurement of LArTPC energy resolution at the MeV scale and provides a pathway for monoenergetic energy calibrations in future experiments using LArTPC detectors.

item.title: TD-Link: A Daisy-Chain Optical Architecture for Integrated Data Readout and Deterministic Timing Distribution in Large-Scale Detector Systems
item.description: arXiv:2607.00904v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: TD-Link is an optical communication architecture that combines high-throughput data readout and sub-nanosecond timing synchronization over a single fiber for large-scale detector systems. It adopts a multidrop daisy-chain ring topology connecting a Data Concentrator to up to sixteen FERS front-end boards per link, with up to eight links per concentrator. Operating at 3.125 Gb/s, TD-Link carries data, synchronization, and control traffic in the same serial stream through a token-based streaming protocol that minimizes per-hop latency and supports on-the-fly payload fragmentation. Deterministic latency is enforced at two levels. On the concentrator, transmitter lanes are aligned by using the half-full flag of the multi-gigabit transceiver (MGT) elastic buffer as a one-bit phase detector: a firmware state machine steps the transmit phase interpolator (PI) until the buffer pointer difference crosses half-depth, locking every lane to the same phase condition. On each front-end board, where the synchronization pulse must also cross from the recovered-clock to the transmit domain, the residual three-to-five-cycle ambiguity of the synchronizer is removed by a calibration-free multiphase oversampling time-to-digital converter (TDC) with 0.8 ns bins, which time-stamps the incoming edge on the transmit time base so that a scheduler regenerates it at a fixed, programmable latency. A Digital Dual Mixer Time Difference (DDMTD) circuit measures the inter-concentrator phase. Tests with CERN PicoTDC-equipped FERS boards show a board-to-board synchronization $\sigma$ of 24 ps on the same ring, 27 ps across transceiver quads, and 28 ps across two cascaded concentrators, against an intrinsic front-end floor of 7 ps. Over more than one thousand cold boots without re-calibration, the boot-to-boot spread of the board-to-board skew stayed below 20 ps, consistent with the 18.6 ps phase-interpolator step.

item.title: Half-Life Measurements of $^{110}$Sn, $^{113}$Sn, $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn, and $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn Produced via Photon Activation of Natural Tin
item.description: arXiv:2606.27064v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We report independent determinations of the ground-state half-lives of $^{110}$Sn, $^{113}$Sn, and the isomeric states $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn (J$^{\pi} = 11/2^{-}$) and $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn (J$^{\pi} = 3/2^{+}$), produced via photon activation of natural tin using a TT-300HE Rhodotron accelerator. The activated samples were monitored over several months using a high-purity germanium (HPGe) detector. Time-dependent $\gamma$-ray spectra were analyzed using Gaussian peak fitting for the \SI{280.49}{keV}, \SI{391.697}{keV}, \SI{158.56}{keV}, and \SI{160.34}{keV} transitions, yielding half-lives of \SI{4.165(25)}{h} for $^{110}$Sn, \SI{116.08(94)}{d} for $^{113}$Sn, \SI{13.95(1)}{d} for $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn, and \SI{39.95(12)}{min} for $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn. Agreement with Nuclear Data Sheets (NDS) recommended values is generally observed for $^{110}$Sn, $^{113}$Sn, and $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn, with deviations consistent within combined uncertainties when quantified using standardized differences (z-scores). In contrast, $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn exhibits a statistically significant deviation from the evaluated value of \SI{13.76(4)}{d}, with a z-score indicating a discrepancy well beyond expected statistical fluctuations. This result suggests a systematic difference warranting further investigation, with potential implications for applications relying on precise decay data, including calibration, dosimetry, and astrophysical modeling.
item.dc:creator: O Nusair, D Devries, M Toto-Gonzalez

item.title: Nonreciprocal Polychromatic Radiation from a Space-Time-Modulated Omega-Topology Meta-Transceiver
item.description: arXiv:2609.38542v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-modulated metasurfaces offer a magnet-free route to nonreciprocal wave control, but existing realizations modulate only the electric response of the structure, and proposals for simultaneous electric-magnetic modulation have so far remained theoretical. We experimentally demonstrate a space-time-periodic meta-transceiver whose omega-topology unit cell integrates varactor-loaded electric (dipole) and magnetic (ring) resonators, both modulated by a common unidirectional traveling-wave bias. This modulation gives rise to two independent, experimentally resolved manifestations of nonreciprocity: on transmit, the incident field is efficiently converted into a polychromatic comb of harmonics that radiate at distinct, bias-reconfigurable angles, while on receive, the same modulation instead suppresses frequency conversion and routes the incoming wave preferentially toward one port over the other. These two effects - nonreciprocal polychromatic conversion and unidirectional wave routing - arise from a single unidirectional space-time modulation but act on distinct physical observables, frequency content and spatial direction, respectively. Measured near the electric resonance with a shared bias, these effects characterize the complete cell and do not separate its electric and magnetic contributions. Our results establish the space-time-modulated omega-topology cell as an experimentally viable platform for reconfigurable, full-duplex nonreciprocal wave transformation.

item.title: Prediction of the thermal neutron response of grain-boundary impedance in Gd-doped ceria based on the radiation-ionic effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.10191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The radiation-ionic effect was recently reported in 3 mol% Gd-doped CeO$_2$ (3GDC): under $^{60}$Co gamma irradiation at 35 Gy/min, the grain-boundary (GB) ionic resistance of a bulk pellet decreased 680-fold at room temperature, because electrons trapped at the GB core lower the space-charge potential. The effect has been demonstrated only with photons. Gd has the largest thermal-neutron capture cross section of any stable element and is also the dopant that creates the GB barrier in GDC, so the same mechanism could link GB impedance to thermal-neutron sensing; whether it does, and under what conditions, has not been examined. Here the thermal-neutron response of 3GDC is modelled with the gamma-calibrated Mott-Schottky/Seager framework, with unmeasured parameters carried as intervals and propagated jointly. Each capture deposits about 50 keV by conversion and Auger electrons within 1 $\mu$m, the remaining 8 MeV leaving as prompt photons; Gd segregation to the GBs adds a factor of only 1-2 because the electron range exceeds the grain size. A thermal flux of $8\times10^{9}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ (6-12$\times10^{9}$) matches the GB-effective generation rate of the 35 Gy/min calibration, and the predicted room-temperature GB resistance ratio is 110 (70-170) at $10^{9}$ and 970 (600-1500) at $10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, falling to 2 at 61 (55-68) and 81 (73-92) $^\circ$C. The neutron case differs from gamma irradiation in three respects: capture events are discrete, so the continuous-source approximation depends on the unmeasured trapped-charge lifetime; self-shielding (mean free path 0.27 mm) makes the response thickness dependent; and capture photons absorbed in the pellet add a gamma term comparable to the local term for pellets of 0.3 mm or more. The intervals are conditional on the model and exclude its structural error. The conditions under which the prediction can be tested are given.
item.dc:creator: Zhongming Zhang

item.title: Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
item.description: arXiv:2610.11892v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The extremely intense pulses of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) have enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to deliver biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work-flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Based on decades of improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to approximately 20 Angstrom, while the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.
